nameStory: The Coastal Mud Shrimp gets its name from its love affair with muddy shorelines, where it spends its entire life burrowing through soft sediment. Unlike true shrimp that swim freely in the water column, these creatures are committed mud-dwellers, earning them the 'mud' part of their name. The 'coastal' designation distinguishes them from their freshwater cousins.
description: The Coastal Mud Shrimp is a small, pale crustacean that looks like a cross between a lobster and a shrimp, but lives its life as an underground architect. These translucent to whitish creatures grow to about 2-3 inches long and have a soft, somewhat flattened body perfect for tunnel life. Their most striking features are their oversized front claws and long antennae that help them navigate their dark, muddy world. Unlike the shrimp you might see at a seafood counter, these are delicate, almost ghost-like creatures with a distinctly un-shrimp-like lifestyle.

idTips.label: Digging claws
idTips.description: Large, flattened front claws that feel sturdy and look like tiny shovels - much more robust than typical shrimp appendages

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Soft, almost jelly-like body that feels delicate to touch, with a translucent to pale cream coloration

idTips.label: Burrow evidence
idTips.description: Look for small, round holes in mud flats with little mounds of expelled sediment nearby - the shrimp's 'doorway'

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About the length of your thumb, with a noticeably flattened body rather than the rounded shape of swimming shrimp

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Exceptionally long, thread-like antennae that can extend well beyond the body length when fully extended

habitat: Found in protected muddy intertidal areas along New England's coast, particularly in salt marshes, quiet bays, and estuaries with fine sediment. They prefer areas where the mud is soft enough to dig but stable enough to maintain tunnel systems, often in zones that stay moist even at low tide. Look for them in the same mudflats where you might find clams and marine worms.

seasonality.spring: Active season begins as waters warm - look for fresh burrow holes and sediment mounds in mudflats during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mud shrimp are most likely to be found near burrow entrances. Best viewing during calm, low tide conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to dig deeper as temperatures drop. Burrow signs may be less obvious on the surface.
seasonality.winter: Retreat deep into their burrows to escape cold - surface activity minimal, though established burrow systems remain.

funFact: These industrious little engineers can completely turn over and process the top layer of an entire mudflat - they're basically underwater earthworms that reshape coastlines one tiny shovelful at a time.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small lobsters or crayfish, but mud shrimp have much more delicate, translucent bodies and those distinctive flattened digging claws rather than the heavy pinchers of lobsters. Remember: if it looks too fragile to survive in a lobster trap, you've probably found a mud shrimp.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, mud shrimp aren't closely related to the shrimp you eat - they're actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs. This is a great example of how common names can be misleading, as 'shrimp' often just means 'small crustacean' in everyday language.
compareHints: As the only Upogebia species commonly found in New England, the Coastal Mud Shrimp is most similar to other burrowing crustaceans like ghost shrimp (Neotrypaea). However, mud shrimp have more robust digging claws and a less ghostly, more substantial appearance. Their burrows are also typically more permanent and well-constructed than those of ghost shrimp.
